Meanwhile busy applications often ask the same database questions thousands of times each hour. A cache keeps recent answers in fast memory; repeated requests skip slow disk reads. A well tuned cache lowers latency, reduces load, and keeps users happy.

However well built, every cache eventually faces staleness. When a row changes in the database, the stored copy may no longer match reality. Teams handle this with expiration timers, explicit invalidation, or write through strategies; each choice trades freshness against speed. Good cache design considers how often data changes and how much delay users tolerate.

Along with this, many firms put a small, fast pool of RAM in front of a main SQL box. Hot rows sit in that pool, so most lookups finish quickly without disk trips. Still, a wary admin monitors hit ratios, adjusts TTL limits, and plans for a crash.

Finally remember that measurement beats guessing; a cache nobody hits wastes memory, so profile queries first and call it done.
